scopeReview: CED FUN-7.A.1: translate verbal rate statements into differential equations, respecting dependent/independent variables, derivative order, units, signs and initial data. Contexts supply every modeling law explicitly; no logistic model, Euler method or advanced differential-equation solution technique is introduced. Hypothetical numerical state tests corroborate mathematical rate relations, not unproved trajectories.
varietyReview: Calibrated proportional growth, signed decay, temperature difference, inflow-minus-outflow, additive interest/deposit rate, acceleration versus velocity, a spatial radius derivative, square-root time rate, initial velocity versus position, verbal variable-square grouping and initial volume versus instantaneous rate. Four state-sample recomputations and seven separate verbal/dimensional reasoning reviews.
repetitionReview: Each prompt and all four options were read separately; distinct tasks/contexts within this set. Cross-topic exact duplicates checked by validator. Semantic similarity and AP difficulty remain judgment calls, not proven by an automated score.

questions.independentReasoning: Independently check the units and calibration: (minute⁻¹)·organisms gives organisms/minute and 0.04·300=12. Doubling the population doubles the rate to 24, while halving it gives 6, as the verbal proportionality requires.
optionReview: This uses the observed rate as the proportionality constant without dividing by population.
The proportionality constant is 12/300=0.04 per minute.
This makes the rate proportional to time rather than population.
This models a constant rate rather than a population-dependent rate.

questions.independentReasoning: At M=10 the rule gives M′=−0.7 mass units/day; at M=20 it gives −1.4, doubling the loss magnitude. The rearranged wrong equation would imply M′=−M/0.07, which has the wrong coefficient. Both direction and scale are independently checked.
optionReview: This describes growth of a positive mass.
This makes the rate depend on elapsed time rather than remaining mass.
The derivative is negative while the remaining positive mass sets its magnitude.
Rearranging this gives a reciprocal decay coefficient, not the stated one.

questions.independentReasoning: Check three separate states: T=100 gives −12 °C/min, T=40 gives −3 °C/min and T=20 gives 0. Each follows the stated difference law and rejects the absolute-temperature and wrong-sign alternatives. No differential-equation solution formula is assumed.
optionReview: This predicts continuing cooling even at the surrounding temperature.
This moves a hotter object away from the surrounding temperature.
This adds rather than subtracts the reference temperature.
The temperature difference from the surroundings, not absolute temperature, sets the signed rate.

questions.independentReasoning: At hypothetical volumes 100,200,250 L, independently compute inflow minus outflow as 3,1,0 L/min. The coefficient 0.02 has inverse-minute units. These state checks corroborate the model; they do not assert the tank visits those volumes at specified times.
optionReview: Net volume rate equals inflow minus outflow.
This counts outflow as an additional inflow.
This omits the stated entering flow.
This replaces the volume-dependent outflow by a time-dependent rule.

questions.independentReasoning: For balances 0,1000,2000 dollars, the stated rules independently give rates 40,50,60 dollars/month. The deposit rate remains 40 regardless of balance. The last option is rejected separately because it asserts a balance formula whose derivative is only 0.01.
optionReview: This incorrectly subjects the deposit rate to another factor 0.01.
The proportional interest rate and constant deposit rate add.
This swaps the constant flow and proportional coefficient.
This gives a balance formula for a different constant-rate model.

questions.independentReasoning: Check physical dimensions: s″ and 9.8 have length/time² units, while coefficient 0.4 has inverse-time units multiplying velocity. At downward velocity 10, the acceleration rule gives 5.8; at zero velocity it gives 9.8. These checks verify sign and derivative roles without solving a second-order equation.
optionReview: This substitutes position for velocity and velocity for acceleration.
This adds the stated resisting velocity term instead of subtracting it.
Acceleration is the second position derivative, and resistance depends on velocity.
This equates position to an expression that does not state the acceleration rule.

questions.independentReasoning: The independently known area formula A=πr² has derivative 2πr, matching both the proportional rule and calibration. Its units are area per length, not area per time. This confirms the model without confusing it with the circumference-like rate expression itself.
optionReview: No time dependence or radius time-rate has been specified.
This makes the observed rate constant instead of proportional to radius.
This equates area to a rate expression rather than modeling its derivative.
The coefficient is (6π)/3=2π and the independent variable is radius.

questions.independentReasoning: Independently evaluate the model at times 0,4,9 to get rates 0,6,9 cm/hour. Changing a hypothetical height at the same time leaves the rate unchanged, as required. The original square-root domain t≥0 is preserved.
optionReview: The proportionality coefficient is 6/√4=3.
This uses the observed rate as the coefficient without dividing by √4.
This makes the rate proportional to t rather than √t.
This changes the independent-variable dependence into height dependence.

questions.independentReasoning: Independently a compatible velocity is s′(t)=2t+3; differentiating it gives 2 and evaluating at 0 gives 3. Any position primitive of that velocity can differ by an arbitrary initial-position constant, confirming why the datum concerns s′ rather than s.
optionReview: This invents position-proportional velocity and replaces initial velocity with position.
A constant rate of velocity change is acceleration, and the initial velocity is a first-derivative value.
This swaps the acceleration and initial-velocity data.
This position formula has constant velocity 2 and zero acceleration.

questions.independentReasoning: At x=2,y=3 the stated rate is 1+2·9=19; the two incorrectly squared formulas give 37 and 13. At x=−1,y=2 it is −3. These independent state substitutions check the grouping and signs. The final algebraic-relation option is rejected separately because it has no rate expression.
optionReview: This also squares x, which the statement does not say.
This squares the wrong variable.
The independent variable multiplies the square of the dependent quantity.
This equates the function value, rather than its rate, to the stated expression.

questions.independentReasoning: At time 0 the two model quantities have different units and values: 12 m³ of volume and 2 m³/hour of rate. An independent compatible volume is 12+2t+1−cos t, whose derivative and initial value reproduce both given statements. No full solution is required to formulate the model.
optionReview: This swaps a volume with a rate and drops the time-varying term.
This treats the rate formula as the volume and the starting volume as a derivative.
The initial condition refers to time 0 and volume 12, not the reverse.
The rate rule and starting volume are recorded in different parts of the model.
